newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran welcomes U.S. remarks, but no thaw yet.
newsitem.headline: Iran welcomes U.S. remarks, but no thaw yet.

text.p: A warmer tone in American remarks about Iran after the Islamic republic's presidential election is unlikely to lead to an early thaw in the iciness between Washington and Tehran, diplomats said on Sunday.
Rapprochement between the two arch-enemies is most likely years away, they said.
"It's very early days yet for 18 years of mutual hatred and distrust to melt away," one diplomat said.

U.S. President Bill Clinton called the election of moderate Shi'ite Moslem cleric Mohammad Khatami as Iran's next president interesting and hopeful and said he had never been pleased about "estrangements" between the United States and Iran.
Khatami said before the May 23 ballot Iran could not shut itself off totally from the rest of the world, however threatened it felt, and it could learn from the West.

But Clinton said big obstacles lay in the way of reconciliation. Since his election in 1993 Clinton has sought to isolate Iran for supporting "terrorism", seeking nuclear arms and trying to wreck Middle East peace efforts.
Tehran denies sponsoring "terrorism", says it legitimately seeks nuclear energy technology but not weaponry, and rejects the U.S.-brokered peace process as a sell-out of Palestinian and Arab rights.
Clinton's comments were seen in Tehran as indicating a gradual change in hostile American policy.
Tehran radio said "Clinton drew his hand towards Iran and his remarks contained signals of friendship and compromise.

"It seems that Clinton's tone speaks of the fact that Washington officials have realised that it is about time for the U.S. to give up its hostile posture in the face of Iran," the state-run radio said.
The U.S. embassy in Tehran, the largest foreign mission in Iran, fell in the 1979 revolution that toppled Washington's closest ally in the region, Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.
Militant students stormed the "den of spies" as the Islamist revolutionaries called the embassy and held 52 Americans hostage for 444 days to demand the Shah's return from exile abroad.

The embassy, occupying prime Tehran real estate, was turned into a military academy for the spearhead Revolutionary Guard. The U.S. seal, neatly picked out in yellow brick at the main gate, was long ago defaced, but most of the graffiti are gone from high walls now topped by barbed wire and lookout posts.
If American diplomats ever return to Iran they will need a new street guide to the capital.
Kennedy Square, Roosevelt Street, Eisenhower Street and all other thoroughfares given American identities under the U.S.-backed Shah were long ago renamed.
But 18 years after the Shah's ouster, signs remain of Iran's ambivalent fascination with all things American.

The Islamic republic earns most of its hard currency from international sales of oil -- it is the world's third largest exporter after Saudi Arabia and Norway -- and the dollar remains the currency of choice for business.

Hotels require foreigners to settle their bills in dollars and staff soliciting tips prefer the greenback -- it can be exchanged on the black market for 4,800 rials compared with the official rate of 3,000.
The Hilton hotel was renamed the Esteghlal (Independence), the Intercontinental became the Laleh (Tulip), and the Sheraton was renamed the Homa, Iran's traditional bird of bliss.
The slogan "Down with USA" is neatly picked out in mosaic tiles in the lobbies of some of them.

In spite of efforts to eradicate all symbols of the "Great Satan" as the revolution's founder Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini called the United States, American icons abound and Iran's conservative clerical establishment pledges to fight a Western cultural onslaught.
Coca-Cola can still be bought in classic green-tinted bottles and counterfeit Ralph Lauren Polo shirts and Calvin Klein jeans are sold in shops and by kerb-side hawkers.
The 240 km of six-lane highways that criss-cross Tehran under a civic development programme begun seven years ago are called expressways and freeways.
Telephone operators are more likely to answer foreign callers in American-accented English than the British version.
And the sports pages of English-language newspapers regularly run U.S. baseball and basketball scores as well as reports of American football.
